# NVFP4 block-scaled dot product on ASAP7

One datapath block of Inkling 2 Small: the inner loop of an expert GEMM in layers 0-39, where
both the weights and the activations are NVFP4. Two variants were generated, verified bit for bit
and taken through place and route: `nvfp4_dot` (weights arrive on ports) and `nvfp4_dot_const`
(the weights of a real expert row are constants). Every number below is in
[`results/silicon.json`](../../results/silicon.json), written by `rtl/nvfp4/run_all.py`.
ASAP7 only; nothing is scaled to another node.

## 1. Result

Placed and routed, ASAP7 RVT, TT 0.70 V 25 C, both at a 1800 ps clock (556 MHz), one
16-value block per clock, power from a gate-level VCD of real tensors (w13 row 0 of layer 0
expert 0 against 8 embedding-derived tokens, no idle clocks):

| | reloadable `nvfp4_dot` | fixed `nvfp4_dot_const`, one 288-block row | reloadable / fixed |
|---|---|---|---|
| cell area (um2), without fill and tap cells | 511.1 | 882.8 | 0.58 |
| cells | 4,548 | 8,234 | 0.55 |
| flip-flops | 273 | 279 | |
| timing at 1800 ps: setup slack / hold slack (ps) | 23.3 / 38.1 | 21.8 / 35.7 | |
| dynamic power (mW) | 1.092 | 1.831 | 0.60 |
| leakage power (uW) | 0.411 | 0.718 | 0.57 |
| energy per 16-value block (pJ) | 1.967 | 3.297 | 0.60 |
| energy per multiply-accumulate (pJ) | 0.1229 | 0.2060 | 0.60 |
| area per multiply-accumulate lane (um2) | 31.94 | 55.18 | 0.58 |
| weights in the module | 16 at a time, none stored | 4,608 hard-wired | |
| area per weight (um2) | 31.94 per weight slot | 0.1916 per hard-wired weight | not like for like |

Over 5 different real rows (same clock, same tokens, each row placed and routed):
reloadable / fixed is **0.58 (0.58 to 0.59, n=5)** for cell area and
**0.60 (0.59 to 0.60, n=5)** for energy per block (median, range).

**Read this before using the ratios.** At equal throughput the fixed variant is *larger* and
uses *more* energy, not less. One block per clock means each of the 16 lanes meets 288 different
weights in turn, so the "constants" become a 288-entry table of 72 bits in logic, and the
multipliers behind it cannot fold; Yosys in fact builds a weight table with registered outputs
in front of the same datapath. The fixed module therefore contains its 4,608 weights
(0.192 um2 each, datapath included), while the reloadable module contains no
weight storage at all: its weights must come from a memory that is not in these numbers.
Constants only fold when a lane always sees the same weight. That case was built too
(a 288-block row whose 16 hard-wired weights are the same in every block, section 8.4): there
reloadable / fixed is **1.13 (1.12 to 1.13, n=2)** for area and
**1.12 (1.11 to 1.13, n=2)** for energy per block.

Clock: both variants close timing at 1800 ps; the critical path of both is the
single-cycle binary32 accumulate. Best period reached in the sweep:
1,616.6 ps (reloadable), 1,699.5 ps (fixed); see 8.2.

## 3. Byte layout and scale formula: what was verified and how

| fact | from the checkpoint bytes | from a serving engine |
|---|---|---|
| Two E2M1 codes per byte, **earlier element in the low nibble** | Per-input-column RMS of the dequantized w13 expert correlates with the real `mlp_norm.weight` of the same layer at r = 0.606 with low-nibble-first and r = -0.001 with the nibbles swapped (null sigma 0.015, 4,608 columns). For w2: 4.5% of neurons have a w2 column aligned beyond 3 sigma with their own w13 gate row with low-nibble-first, 0.35% with the nibbles swapped (chance: 0.27%) | TokenSpeed `block_scaled.py`: `packed = code[:, 0::2] \| (code[:, 1::2] << 4)`, decode `(values & 15, values >> 4)` |
| Code = sign bit 3, magnitude index bits 2:0 into (0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6); `0x8` is -0 | Both zero codes occur: 3.43% `0x0` and 3.44% `0x8` of w13. All 1,327,104 blocks of the w13 expert have 6.0 as their largest code (1,327,104), as "nearest, block maximum to 6" predicts | TokenSpeed `_fp4_round` and `_decode_values` |
| Block scale is `float8_e4m3fn`: NaN = `0x7F`, `0xFF`; no infinity; max 448; subnormals `m * 2^-9` | Real scales use bytes 101..126 only (values 52 to 448); 0 zero, 0 subnormal, 0 negative, 0 NaN bytes in w13; same for w2 | all 256 bytes decoded identically by `torch.float8_e4m3fn` (True); encoder identical to torch's cast on 2,000,126 values (True) |
| **Weight = code x block scale x amax[expert] / outer_scale_denominator**; the denominator stored in the checkpoint is 2688 (= 6 x 448) | max over the expert of \|code\| x block scale is 2688 = the denominator, so the formula returns max\|w\| = 0.08124460 against stored amax 0.08124460 (w13); 0.11775652 against 0.11775653 (w2) | TokenSpeed reference kernel: `(amax_token * a13[expert]) * (1536 * d13[0]).reciprocal()` |
| Activation = code x block scale x amax[token] / 1536, block scale by four-over-six | not in the checkpoint (run-time) | `reference_block_quantize` executed from TokenSpeed's source at commit `a439df467540`: our quantizer gives identical codes, scales and amax on 1,290 token rows in 5 sets (pass: True) |
| w13 rows interleave gate and up: rows 2i, 2i+1 belong to neuron i | the w2-column alignment above only appears for this pairing (tested against a split-halves pairing while exploring; not in the JSON) | TokenSpeed `gate_up[:, 0::2]`, `[:, 1::2]` |

Only one expert was fetched whole; the layout checks were run on layer 0 expert 0. TokenSpeed's
`inkling2.py` and its test only validate dtypes and shapes; the arithmetic is in its kernel
package (`tokenspeed-kernel/.../ops/moe/block_scaled.py`), which is what was read and executed.

## 4. Arithmetic and micro-architecture

[SPEC.md](SPEC.md) has the definition. In short: the 16 products of a block are summed exactly
as integers, multiplied exactly by the two E4M3 scales (the product always fits 19 bits, so the
block term is an exact binary32 number), and added to a binary32 accumulator, one IEEE
round-to-nearest-even addition per block, in block order. Five register stages, one block per
clock, the accumulate in one clock. NaN scales give `0x7FC00000`; overflow gives infinity.

Other checks:

* **Two references.** The NumPy float32 reference and a pure-integer model of the RTL adder agree
  on every vector they were both run on (asserted in `verify.py` and in the test suite).
* **Second simulator.** Icarus Verilog: 96 real vectors on the reloadable module
  (0 mismatches), 8 on the fixed one (0).
* **Overflow.** Not reachable from the ports (terms are below 2^27), so a testbench hook overwrites
  the accumulator register and places one large binary32 term in front of the adder (Icarus):
  10 cases (max + max, -max - max, max + half an ulp, which rounds up into infinity, max + a
  quarter ulp, which does not, exact cancellation, infinity followed by a NaN scale, ...), then
  11 ordinary terms. RTL = integer model = NumPy float32 in all (True).
* **After place and route.** Every routed netlist was simulated at gate level (Icarus, ASAP7 cell
  models) on its power workloads and compared with the reference: all bit-exact
  (True, 13 designs).

## 6. Reference against PyTorch

`torch.nn.functional.linear` (CPU, 2.15.0+cpu, 4 threads) on dequantized floats (code x block scale, which
float32 holds exactly) against the reference, for the whole real expert:

| set | outputs | bit-identical to torch | worst relative error | worst error / sum of \|terms\| | engine = exact value | torch = exact value | torch batch of 1 = torch full batch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| w13 (4608 x 4608) x 512 embedding-derived tokens | 2,359,296 | 100.00% | 0 | 0 | 100.00% | 100.00% | 100.00% |
| w13 (4608 x 4608) x 128 heavy-tailed synthetic tokens | 589,824 | 100.00% | 0 | 0 | 100.00% | 100.00% | 100.00% |
| w2 (4608 x 2304) x 256 SwiGLU outputs of the real w13 | 1,179,648 | 100.00% | 0 | 0 | 100.00% | 100.00% | 100.00% |
| random codes and random finite scales, 512 rows x 64 tokens (rounding occurs) | 32,768 | 8.95% | 0.0123 | 4.97e-07 | 13.16% | 13.73% | 10.01% |

Stated tolerance: error below 1e-06 of the sum of absolute terms (pass: True).

* On the real expert with real-looking tokens the two are **bit-identical, and both are exact**:
  with real block scales every term is a multiple of a small power of two and every partial sum
  stayed below 2^24 of that unit, so no addition rounded and the order of additions could not matter.
* They stop being identical as soon as additions round (last row: random codes and random scale
  bytes). The engine adds 288 exact block terms in block order; torch adds 4,608 products in
  whatever order its BLAS kernel uses (vectorised partial sums, possibly fused multiply-add).
  Different association, different rounding, both within a few units in the last place of the
  running sum. The same row shows that torch on CPU is itself not batch invariant there.
* With the second-level scales folded into the operands first (true float dequantization, then
  `linear`), operands are rounded to 24 bits before the products, so results differ from
  engine x outer scale by up to 5.6e-08 of the sum of absolute terms (median relative
  error 3.2e-07); the relative error is unbounded where a sum cancels to zero.

## 7. Determinism and batch invariance

48 probe dot products were driven at batch sizes 1, 2, 3, 8, 32 and 128, at the first, middle and
last position of the batch, back to back and with random idle gaps (30 placements each), the
other tokens of the batch random: reloadable engine (a batch = tokens streamed against one weight
row) and the 8-row fixed module (a batch = tokens streamed through the same hard-wired rows).
12,960 probe results; each probe produced exactly 1 distinct bit pattern, equal
to the reference (pass: True).

Why: the result of a row depends only on that row's blocks. The accumulator starts from +0 for
every row, the reduction order is fixed (exact sum inside a block, then one rounded addition per
block in block order), there is no state shared between rows and no data-dependent scheduling;
the per-token second-level scale keeps quantization independent of the batch as well.

## 8. Silicon

### 8.1 Flow, constraints, tools

**Place and route ran.** The Docker daemon was started by hand (`dockerd`, data root in scratch)
and the free image `openroad/orfs` pulled; every design went through the OpenROAD-flow-scripts
ASAP7 platform: Yosys/ABC synthesis (flattened), floorplan, placement, clock-tree synthesis,
global and detailed routing (violations left by the router, summed over all 13 designs:
0), fill, OpenRCX extraction,
final OpenSTA timing with propagated clocks. Yosys + ABC + OpenSTA without layout was the
fallback and was not needed, except for the 8-row slices (8.5), which were only synthesized.

* Library: asap7sc7p5t RVT standard cells, NLDM, TT corner (0.70 V, 25 C); ORFS CORNER=TC. ORFS's default for ASAP7 is the fast corner; the typical one was chosen.
* Constraint (ps), the same for every design:

```
current_design <top>
set clk_period <clock_ps>
create_clock -name clk -period $clk_period [get_ports clk]
set_input_delay  [expr {0.2 * $clk_period}] -clock clk [all_inputs -no_clocks]
set_output_delay [expr {0.2 * $clk_period}] -clock clk [all_outputs]
```

* Floorplan: core utilization 50%, placement density 0.6, square core.
* Power: `report_power` of OpenSTA on the routed netlist with SPEF parasitics and the VCD of a
  zero-delay gate-level simulation; 15,433 pins annotated from the VCD, 2 not.
* Tools: Yosys 0.68+post (git sha1 UNKNOWN, Release, GNU /usr/local/bin/wrapped-cc/g++ 15.2.0); OpenSTA 3.1.0 (inside OpenROAD); OpenROAD binary of openroad/orfs@sha256:31c5fd29e541059e36ad87b197ece981c04d2ce3a1f2035976fe266ec0e521cb (reports its version as 'unknown'); KLayout 0.30.12;
  Verilator 5.020 2024-01-01 rev (Debian 5.020-1); Icarus Verilog version 12.0 (stable) (); host Yosys 0.33 (git sha1 2584903a060) (host; lint only); Python 3.13.18, NumPy 2.5.4, torch 2.15.0+cpu.

### 8.4 How many different weights a lane sees decides the answer

The same generator was run on 288-block rows whose 16 hard-wired weights are the **same in every
block** (one block of w13 row 0 repeated; two different blocks), placed and routed at 1800 ps.
Function, row length, tokens and throughput are those of 8.3, and the reloadable module
(511.1 um2) was given the identical work, the same repeated weights held on its weight pins.

| distinct blocks the row cycles through | distinct weights | designs | fixed area (um2) | fixed flip-flops | area R/F | fixed pJ / block | reloadable pJ / block, same work | energy R/F |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 16 | 2 | 453.7 (450.3 to 457.2, n=2) | 204 (202 to 206, n=2) | 1.13 (1.12 to 1.13, n=2) | 1.636 (1.617 to 1.655, n=2) | 1.831 (1.829 to 1.832, n=2) | 1.12 (1.11 to 1.13, n=2) |
| 288 | 4,608 | 5 | 878.1 (871.0 to 882.8, n=5) | 279 (279 to 279, n=5) | 0.58 (0.58 to 0.59, n=5) | 3.284 (3.269 to 3.308, n=5) | 1.958 (1.943 to 1.968, n=5) | 0.60 (0.59 to 0.60, n=5) |

* **One distinct block** is the case where every lane always multiplies by the same weight: the
  E2M1 multipliers fold into wiring, zero weights drop out of the adder tree, the weight registers
  disappear and the weight side of the scale product is a constant. The accumulator is still the
  full binary32 one. This is the like-for-like "same function, constants folded" figure:
  reloadable / fixed 1.13 (1.12 to 1.13, n=2) in area and 1.12 (1.11 to 1.13, n=2) in
  energy per block. The gain is bounded because what remains (adder tree, 12 x 8 scale
  multiplier, normaliser and above all the binary32 accumulator) does not shrink with constants.
  On the reloadable side this workload holds the weight pins still, so the energy ratio already
  excludes weight-pin toggling.
* **Every further distinct block is a table entry.** From 1 to 288 distinct blocks the fixed
  module grows by 0.092 um2 per distinct hard-wired weight (4.5 bits each). The reloadable
  module does not grow; its weights are somewhere else, and that memory is not in these numbers.
  Tables of 4, 16 and 72 blocks were generated and verified in RTL but not placed and routed.
* A design that hard-wires weights and gives every weight its own lane (fully spatial) is the
  1-block point repeated, plus the activation distribution such a layout needs; a design that
  time-multiplexes 16 lanes over a hard-wired row is the 288-block point. The study should not use
  one ratio for both.
* **A trap that was measured and set aside.** Rows that are only one block *long* were built first
  (3 designs): area ratio 1.56 (1.50 to 1.59, n=3), energy ratio 1.32 (1.27 to 1.33, n=3). In those
  the accumulator always adds to zero and synthesis removes the binary32 adder from the fixed
  module, so the ratios overstate the saving. They are kept in the JSON under
  `rows_of_one_block_accumulator_optimized_away`, not used here.

### 8.5 Eight rows sharing one activation stream (synthesis only)

`nvfp4_dot_x8` (eight weight streams) and `nvfp4_dot_const_x8` (w13 rows 16..23 of layer 0 expert 0
hard-wired) were verified in RTL simulation (32,768 and 110,936 row results, 0 mismatches) and
synthesized with the same ORFS Yosys/ABC step, **not placed and routed** (the fixed one is
61,648 cells and its routing was not attempted, to keep the run time bounded).
Post-synthesis cell area: reloadable 3,761.6 um2 (34,543 cells), fixed 6,309.2 um2
(61,648 cells): reloadable / fixed 0.596. Sharing the activation registers and
the block counter across rows makes the 8-row reloadable module 0.952 of eight single-row
ones and the 8-row fixed module 0.882 of eight median single rows
(0.171 um2 per hard-wired weight). No timing or power for these.

### 8.6 Context

A published 28 nm synthesis of an NVFP4 MAC block (arXiv 2603.28765 (as quoted to us; not re-read here)) reports
21.5 pJ per 16-element block at 524 MHz in 0.024 mm2; this reloadable block on ASAP7 is
1.97 pJ per block at 556 MHz in 0.000511 mm2 of cells. Different node, library,
function boundary and method, so this is context, not a comparison; that paper was not re-read here.

## 9. What was not done, and what to keep in mind

* **Glitches are not in the power numbers.** The VCDs come from zero-delay gate-level simulation,
  so each net toggles at most once per clock. Real adder trees and multipliers glitch; expect the
  combinational share to be higher in silicon. The ratios between variants are less affected than
  the absolute values.
* **Activations are real-looking, not real.** Real weights, real embedding rows and real norm
  weights were used, but no forward pass of the model; power depends on activation statistics
  (section 8.3, last table).
* **ASAP7 is a predictive academic kit**, the libraries are the typical corner at 0.70 V, RVT only,
  and no multi-corner sign-off, IR-drop or electromigration closure was done. One placement seed
  per design; a spread from the tools themselves was not measured.
* **Clock.** The accumulate was left in one clock on purpose (it is a recurrence). It was not
  hand-optimised (single-path adder, no leading-zero anticipation); a faster adder would raise
  both variants' clock equally. Fmax is bracketed by the constraints tried, not searched finely.
* **The fixed variant is one micro-architecture**: a per-row table selected by a block counter in
  front of the shared datapath. Mask ROM or a fully spatial layout are different designs; the
  1-block table (8.4) is the closest measured point to the spatial one, without the activation
  routing such a design needs. Two codings of the table (a case statement, an indexed constant)
  synthesized to 902.6 and 893.8 um2 (row 0; the second figure is from a one-off run, not in the JSON).
* **Glitch-aware power was attempted and dropped**: an SDF-annotated gate-level run in Icarus did
  not stay bit-exact (conditional arcs rejected, flip-flop instances not matched), so it is not used.
* **Wide slices** were synthesized, not routed. **Overflow** is reached only through a testbench
  hook that writes internal registers (section 5), in Icarus, on the RTL.
* **One expert** was fetched whole (layer 0, expert 0), plus 64-row samples of six others; the
  fixed-weight spread is over rows of one expert.
* **Planned and not run**, to finish on time: a third clock point (1700 ps), a third repeated-block
  design, tables of 4, 16 and 72 blocks, place and route of the 8-row slices.
* The Verilator harness and the file-driven testbench assume 16-value blocks (64-bit code words);
  the generator itself is generic in the block size.
* Not committed, not pushed. Place-and-route work files are in scratch, not in the repo.

## 10. Assumptions

1. The engine's arithmetic is this study's definition (exact block sum, exact scaling, one binary32
   round-to-nearest-even addition per block, block order). GPUs accumulate in FP32 in an order
   their kernels choose; on the real tensors tried here the order does not change the bits.
2. Second-level scales are applied outside the block, once per output.
3. Rows are streamed one block per clock with no back-pressure; memory, control and the SwiGLU
   between the two projections are outside the block.
4. Power is at full utilisation (a block on every clock) unless a workload says otherwise.
5. Negative, zero, subnormal and NaN scales are handled although real weights use none of them.

## 11. Reproduce

```
python tools/fetch_expert_fixture.py            # network; rewrites data/fixtures/ (SHA-256 in manifest.json)
python rtl/nvfp4/run_all.py                     # RTL, verification, place and route (Docker + openroad/orfs), power, this page
python rtl/nvfp4/run_all.py --skip-pnr          # reuse finished place-and-route runs
python -m pytest -q tests/test_rtl_nvfp4.py     # the 2-second subset
```
